newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel keeps pressure on PLO despite diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Israel keeps pressure on PLO despite diplomacy.

text.p: Israel on Monday stuck to its tough stance toward Palestinians amid a flurry of diplomacy aimed at rescuing peace moves thrown into deep crisis by the twin suicide bombings in a Jerusalem market.

The European Union's peace envoy said he would try to persuade Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to lift stringent measures levelled against Palestinians after Wednesday's bombing that killed 13 people and wounded 170.

"We cannot really understand some measures that instead of bringing security are bringing insecurity," envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos said at a Gaza news conference with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. He was to meet Netanyahu later in the day.
Arafat, who was to see Jordan's King Hussein in Amman on Monday afternoon to discuss the deepening crisis, said:
"These are collective punishment against the Palestinian people aimed to humiliate the Palestinian people, but they must know that no one can humiliate the Palestinian people."
But Netanyahu, who on Sunday put the world on notice that Israel's peacemaking with the PLO begun in 1993 might be nearing the end of the road, refused to stand down.
"The Palestinian Authority must decide what type of regime it is, a regime that fights terrorism like Jordan and Egypt, or a regime that encourages terrorism like Iraq and Iran.
"If it decides to continue as a regime that does not fight terrorism...we will continue our measures," Netanyahu said as he went into a meeting with U.S. Republican Senator Phil Gramm.
Gramm, a staunch supporter of Israel, said Congress might not renew aid to the Palestinian Authority.

"Authorisation for Palestinian aid as you know expires on August 12. It will not be renewed by the United States Congress in my opinion unless the Palestinians begin living up to the commitments they've made," Gramm said.

Netanyahu's government suspended peace talks with the Palestinians in reaction to Wednesday's attack and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, preventing tens of thousands of Palestinians from reaching their jobs in the Jewish state.
It also threatened to enter Palestinian self-rule areas to fight militants if Arafat did not do the job.

Palestinians, who suspended security cooperation with Israel after Netanyahu launched a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March, say they have nonetheless worked to foil attacks by militants opposed to the peace process.

A leaflet issued in the name of the Islamic Hamas group claimed responsibility for the bombings at an Israeli market in Jerusalem, although both Israeli and Palestinian officials say they are not sure of its authenticity.
Arafat spokesman Ahmed Tibi said that in light of doubts over the bombers' identities, Netanyahu owed Arafat an apology.

"I think the whole campaign against the Palestinian Authority and against Chairman Arafat personally is unnecessary, damaging and inappropriate and Mr Benjamin Netanyahu will do well to phone the chairman and apologise," he told Israel Radio.
On Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet Israel would not honour peace deals it signed with Arafat's Palestinian Authority unless Arafat cracked down on militants.
He later told CBS-TV's "Face the Nation": "The whole peace is at stake. Arafat must make a choice and make it now."
Before winning elections in May 1996, Likud leader Netanyahu opposed interim peace deals reached by the Labour party. In his campaign, however, he said he would honour signed accords.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy is to go to Egypt on Tuesday for talks on the crisis with President Hosni Mubarak. He told Israel Radio: "Israel doesn't want the collapse of the Authority...but the Authority has taken upon itself the responsibility...to take action against terrorism."
U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross is expected to visit the region later this week. Analysts say he will have a tough time just getting Palestinians and Israelis into face-to-face talks.

Israel on Monday demolished three illegally built homes in Arab East Jerusalem. Palestinians say it is hard to obtain building permits and that demolitions are aimed at squeezing them out of Jerusalem.

Israel's Jerusalem Mayor Ehud Olmert calls illegal Arab building a "cancer" that threatens Israel's hold on the city. Israel occupied East Jerusalem in 1967 and vows never to cede an inch of it. Palestinians want it as capital of a future state.
